65.t: Sequence of record labels after Decca
65.s: After Decca he recorded for Continental, Verne, Mercury, Columbia under Mitch Miller, and later Tico.
65.ch: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
65.q: Continental, and from Verne we went to - no to Mercury, and from Mercury we went with Mitch Miller. Mitch Miller joined Columbia, worked for Columbia, and then we finished with Columbia. We made all - - two-year contract we had with Columbia we made in one month, because they want to discontinue…

65.t: Signing with Verne Records and the Rapping Day name
65.s: Cuevas's Verne label recorded Miguelito, Guerra, Trio San Juan and Machito; Guerra's Rapping Day was a pseudonym.
65.ch: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
65.q: Well, Miguelito Valdes was free-lancing so this company, Verne, owned by Cuevas, he approached us. Miguelito, Marcelino Guerra, Trio San Juan, myself,/and he wanted to make a 'catalog so that particular time we recorded with and a few other bands

591.s: A disappointing Berlin session with a trumpet player who would not play the style wanted.
591.q: Well, I recorded in Berlin in 53, and I was very disappointed. I've made one record with, you know, Frank Burley's blues or something. Yeah. And the other side, I forgot what it was. And I talked to the trumpet player that was supposed to make this record for me. I told him why they wanted it, and…

194.t: The Ebb session and label owner Leona Rupe
194.s: He recalls doing another session for a label run by Leona Rupe, with Dick Surgeon as A&R man, and letting others pick the musicians.
194.q: Well, Dick didn't, you know. Yeah. Yeah. So she was at the session? Yeah, it was the session being done for her. Right. Which I thought was for Dick Surgeon, which wasn't. He was just there to boost me along to, for her. Oh, yeah.

51.t: The Spikes Brothers, the Dreamland and the first records
51.s: The Spikes Brothers bought the Dreamland and ran a record shop; Ory recalls the first recording equipment he saw.
51.q: Spikes Brothers. Those are the ones Manuel was telling you about had a dreamland, you know. Yeah. We went to work for us. We left the other place and shift around. They were musicians too, you know.

223.t: Producing Jimmy Rowles's Weather in a Jazz Vane
223.s: His first production credit, for a label connected to Bob Keane with Lou Adler and Herb Alpert there; Rowles sang on the date.
223.q: Yeah, okay. He had a couple of labels, and this was one of them. It was run by a guy who made a fortune in the aircraft instrument business, altimeters and stuff like that. He eventually bought it from Keane, or something. Anyway, I was working for him. He didn‟t know anything about music. I‟m not…

371.t: A&R man Teddy Reig and Teddie's memory
371.s: Jones recalls the heavy A&R man who worked for Savoy before Ozzie Cadena.
371.q: Savoy, yes. But, there is also that other company…Okay, so it’s mainly Savoy. But, that was before Ozzie Cadena came along, you know? Teddie has a fantastic memory. She remembers telephone numbers from 1954! (Laughs)

426.t: Acetate playbacks and the sound-wave label artist
426.s: He made acetate playbacks with a printed label designed by a newspaper artist friend.
426.ch: Sherwood, big bands and sound concept
426.q: You mean about Debut. Yeah I used to make playbacks, acetate playbacks, and I had a bunch of labels I used to stick on so you knew what the label was, what the record was. I had a cart of them out here from the printer. Oh there is the house…jeez.

80.t: The 'Jealous Woman Blues' date with no drums for Frankie's label
80.s: At a Sansom Street Philadelphia club a young Italian fan arranged a recording for the Mammoth label, but the new drummer lacked drums, and Autrey considers it the worst date of his career.
80.ch: Postwar years, accident and lean times
80.q: -- I think it would be kind of nice, because I met a nice little guy, little Italian fellow, Frankie -- what was Frankie's last name? Anyways, he was

230.t: The Cherokee date for an independent label after the Decca falling-out
230.s: After fighting with Decca's Dave Kapp, Barnet recorded Cherokee, Redskin Rhumba and others for a short-lived label whose name he cannot recall.
230.q: Oh, '44, yeah. '43 and '44. No, there wasn't any recording strike. We recorded -- oh, I know what was wrong. I got into a fight with -- it was with Decca, and I got in a fight with Dave Kapp and we mutually agreed to sever all connections. That was -- and I was not with any record company at the…

4.t: Paul Williams draws the Sunshine label
4.s: The California mission and palm trees on the Sunshine label were drawn by the later architect Paul Williams, who wanted to join the record company.
4.ch: Central Avenue clubs, Nordskog, Sheffield and Music Town
4.q: Yeah. He was...he wanted to be in my company-- my record company. You know he was crazy about music and stuff, and he come down there, and he drew that picture for me.

380.t: "Ode to a Giant" and Eddie Laguna's small concerts
380.s: He explains the blues made up on the spot for the Sunset label and talks of small concerts recorded without commercial thought.
380.q: Oh, yeah. I'm looking here, The Red Callender Six. That was with Herbie Haymer, Arnold Ross, Les Paul, Shadow Wilson. That's when we did "These Foolish Things" and an original, "Ode To A Giant," "Get Happy" featuring Sweets Edison, "I Cover The Waterfront" which featured Sweets, and "Lady, Be Good."

382.t: Transition to long-playing records and sorting the Period albums
382.s: Hughes and Maxine try to straighten out the three Period LPs and the Jazztone reissue.
382.q: Jazztone, which is a record that you have in your collection. We've seen that one. And you also have one of the Period albums which is Period SLPl207. Excuse me, SPL.

70.s: Jackson names Brunswick, Victor, Columbia and Vocalion as the main labels.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: Well, it's according. You had Brunswick, you had Victor, you had Columbia, you had Vocalion. Those were, really, the main companies --

232.t: The Frisco label and Fields' earlier records
232.s: Fields recorded Butches Blues on his own Frisco label, with a Golden Gate Bridge design, before the national success of In The Mood.
232.ch: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
232.q: I had one number, while you're mentioning it, that I did on Butches Blues (phonetic spelling), and I did it originally just on Frisco, I had my own company, I did have distribution but then another outfit, when it began to get played, heard about it and asked if they could release it for us and I…

238.t: Phoning Dexter and her home recordings
238.s: After hesitating she called Dexter, met him, mentioned her home records made on a Packard Bell, and learned her brother Joe had played him some without telling her.
238.q: Capitol Records wanted to hear from me, wanted me to get in touch with him. Well, I didn't do it right away. I hesitated. It was two or three days. Because I had been disappointed. And I said, well, two or three days after that, I said well, I'll give Mr. Dexter a call. So when I called, well his…
